Adam Loy :::{.medium} Stat 230 - Spring 2026 ::: ## Welcome 👋 - I'm Adam (he/him) - I teach statistics & data science - I'm interested in statistics education, data visualization, and R programming ::: {.cell} ::: ## Your turn - Form groups based on value (2, 3, 4...) of the card dealt - Introduce yourself to your group - Share at least one thing other than just your name and major # Regression Review ## Key ideas from intro {.nostretch} ::::: columns ::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-slides-slr-review_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"}
- Describe the scatterplot - Write the equation of the regression line - Interpret the slope and intercept - Make a prediction ::: ::::: ## Q: Describe the scatterplot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-slides-slr-review_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} :::{.small} ::: {.conceptest} 1. There is a strong, positive, linear association between temperature and number of rides. 2. There is a moderate, positive, linear association between temperature and number of rides. ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} :::{.small} ::: {.conceptest} 3. There is a moderate, positive, non-linear association between temperature and number of rides. 4. There is a moderate, positive, linear association between temperature and number of rides, but there are a few extreme outliers. ::: ::: ::: ::::: ## Q: Write the equation of the regression line Step 1: Read the set up on the handout Step 2: Which of the following is the correct equation of the regression line?
::: {.conceptest} 1. $y = 520.1 - 18.7x$ 1. $\widehat{y} = 520.1 - 18.7x$ 1. $y = -18.7 + 520.1x$ 1. $\widehat{y} = -18.7 + 520.1x$ ::: ## Q: Interpret the slope in context ::: {.conceptest} 1. For every one-hour increase in sleep duration, the model predicts an average decrease of 18.7 milliseconds in reaction time. 1. For every one-millisecond decrease in reaction time, the model predicts an average increase of 18.7 hours of sleep. 1. If a student gets 0 hours of sleep, their reaction time is predicted to be -18.7 milliseconds. 1. Getting more sleep causes a person's reaction time to drop by exactly 18.7 milliseconds every night. ::: ## Q: Interpret the intercept in context ::: {.conceptest} 1. Yes; it represents the average reaction time (520.1 ms) for all participants in the study regardless of how much they slept. 1. Yes; it represents the predicted reaction time (520.1 ms) for a participant who gets 0 hours of sleep. 1. No; while it represents the predicted reaction time for 0 hours of sleep, this is an example of extrapolation because 0 hours was outside the observed range of 3–9 hours. 1. No; the intercept is just a mathematical placeholder and never carries physical meaning in social science statistics. ::: ## Q: Make a prediction The researchers are asked to predict the reaction time for a healthy young adult who sleeps 10 hours per night. Using the regression equation $\widehat{y}=520.1−18.7x$, which of the following is the most statistically sound conclusion? ::: {.conceptest} 1. The prediction is 333.1 ms; this is highly reliable because 10 hours is very close to the studied range. 1. The prediction is 333.1 ms, but it is unreliable because we cannot assume the linear trend continues beyond the 3–9 hour range. 1. The model cannot be used at all because 10 hours of sleep is biologically impossible for a young adult. 1. The slope would likely change from negative to positive at 10 hours, making the reaction time 520.1 + 18.7(10). ::: ## Q: Purpose of randomization Why did the researchers randomly assign the 65 participants to specific sleep conditions (3–9 hours) rather than just letting them sleep as much as they usually do? ::: {.conceptest} 1. To ensure that the participants in the 3-hour group were already "short sleepers" who are used to exhaustion. 1. To make the sample size in each sleep condition exactly equal, which is a requirement for linear regression. 1. To balance out potential confounding variables (like caffeine intake or baseline fitness) across the different sleep groups. 1. To increase the "power" of the study by ensuring the results can be generalized to the entire U.S. population. ::: ## Q: Generalizing results Can the results of this specific study be generalized to all young adults in the United States? ::: {.conceptest} 1. Yes; because the study used a controlled laboratory setting and random assignment, the results apply to everyone. 1. Yes; because the age range (18–25) is a standard definition for "young adults" across the country. 1. No; because the 65 participants were "recruited" (likely a convenience sample from one college), they may not represent the diversity of all U.S. young adults. 1. No; the sample size of 65 is mathematically too small to ever represent a population as large as the United States. ::: # Regression in Stat 230 ## Simple Linear Regression Model $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i$ where $\varepsilon_i \overset{\rm iid}{\sim} N (0, \sigma^2)$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-slides-slr-review_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ## Simple Linear Regression Model $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i$ where $\varepsilon_i \overset{\rm iid}{\sim} N (0, \sigma^2)$
- Linear relationship between $x$ and $y$ - Errors are independent and identically distributed (iid) - Errors are normally distributed - Errors have mean 0 - Variance of the errors doesn't depend on $x$ ## Notation Mean function: $\quad E(Y|X)=\mu\{Y|X\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$
Fitted model equation: $\quad \widehat{Y}_i = \widehat{\mu}\{Y|X\} = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i$ # Overview of Stat 230 ## Overview of the term Goal: Develop models to answer research questions ```{mermaid} timeline %%{init: {'theme':'neutral'}}%% Weeks 1-2 : Simple linear regression : Review : Inference : Model diagnostics Weeks 3-5 : Multiple linear regression : Interpretation : Inference : Model diagnostics : Model selection Weeks 6-8 : Logistic regression : Interpretation : Inference : Model diagnostics : Model selection Weeks 9-10 : Poisson regression : Interpretation : Inference ``` ## Typical week :::::{.r-fit-text} :::: {.r-hstack} ::: { style="background: #ffd24f; width: 33%; height: 90%; margin: 20px; padding: 0.5em; border-radius: 5px;"} **Monday** - Pre-class reading/video - Reflection questions

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
